identity.description: Unsupervised anomaly detection by random isolation: an ensemble of trees with random feature + random threshold splits on small subsamples. Anomalies are 'few and different', so they separate in FEWER splits — the anomaly score is the normalized average path length to isolation. No labels, no density model, near-linear cost.

consumes.note: unsupervised — no target; fit on the population, score every row

emits.note: normalized average isolation path length; driver flips sklearn's sign so HIGHER = more anomalous (score_samples natively returns lower = more abnormal). Threshold-free — the honest primary output
predict()'s inlier/outlier label — a POLICY artifact of the contamination threshold applied to the score, not a learned class; prefer consuming the raw anomaly-score downstream

n_estimators.note: scores are averages over random trees — more trees means lower score variance

max_samples.note: 'auto' = min(256, n) — the paper's ψ=256 subsample; small subsamples are a feature (they REDUCE masking/swamping), not a cost cut

contamination.note: a POLICY choice, not a fit choice: it only sets the label threshold on the already-fitted score function — the trees and scores are identical for any value. Never tune it as a fit hyperparameter; set it (or a downstream threshold) from review capacity / cost of a false alarm

max_features.note: per-tree feature subsampling; below 1.0 can help when many features are noise

invariances.why: split thresholds are drawn uniformly on each feature's OWN observed range — an affine rescale maps that uniform draw onto the rescaled range, leaving isolation-depth distributions identical
unlike gain-optimized trees, thresholds are uniform on VALUE not on order — a nonlinear monotone map (log) re-spreads mass along the range and changes which points isolate quickly
the sklearn implementation rejects NaN at fit and score time — no default-direction handling exists for isolation trees
the sklearn estimator requires a numeric matrix; categoricals must be pre-encoded
no density or distributional form is fit — the only premise is structural: anomalies are FEW and DIFFERENT, hence easier to isolate by random cuts
each tree fits on a ~256-row subsample by design, so cost and behavior are nearly flat from small datasets to millions of rows
points outside the training range fall past the learned split ranges and isolate in very few steps → maximal scores; extrapolation IS the detection mechanism working as intended

featureStats.why: heavy-tailed marginals produce many legitimately extreme rows with short isolation paths — extremeness gets conflated with anomaly and false positives inflate
each split picks ONE random feature, so as p grows with few informative dimensions, splits are wasted on noise and isolation depth loses its signal — the known iForest high-dimension weakness
large exact-duplicate masses (sentinel values, system defaults) deepen paths around them and can mask true anomalies hiding near dense clumps

modelMetrics.why: a distinct high-score tail in the anomaly-score distribution is what makes any threshold defensible; a unimodal blob means no few-and-different structure was found
scores are means of path lengths over RANDOM trees — per-row instability across seeds means n_estimators is too low for the tree-to-tree variance

edgeCases.condition: contamination set with no cost/capacity basis
edgeCases.behavior: the flagged-outlier COUNT is forced to match the setting regardless of what the data contains
edgeCases.note: surface the score distribution and make the threshold an explicit reviewed policy, not a default

edgeCases.behavior: grouped anomalies form their own dense pocket, isolate slowly, and score near inliers
edgeCases.note: small max_samples mitigates; still flag when score_separation is weak

edgeCases.behavior: no informative splits exist — path lengths are uniform and scores carry no signal

driver.constructor: IsolationForest(n_estimators=..., max_samples=..., contamination=..., max_features=..., random_state=..., n_jobs=...)
driver.wrapperNeeds: negate score_samples() so higher = more anomalous before emitting anomaly-score (sklearn's convention is lower = more abnormal); pass predict()'s ±1 through as the thresholded label emission
driver.threadSafety: n_jobs-parallel fit and scoring; scoring a fitted model is thread-safe

placementClaims.why: the sklearn estimator rejects NaN outright — rows must be complete before fit/score
thresholds are uniform on the raw value range, so de-skewing a heavy-tailed feature re-spreads its mass and reduces extremeness-driven false positives (the marginal_kurtosis signal, acted on)
scale-insensitive by mechanism — affine rescaling leaves isolation structure unchanged, so standardization is wasted compute
numeric-matrix requirement — categoricals must be integer/one-hot encoded before random-threshold splits apply
